blogs.title: Volcano v1.16 Released: NamespaceQueue, fairshare, and a broader HyperNode ecosystem
blogs.content: Posted on October 28, 2026 by Volcano Maintainers Volcano v1.16.0 is available . v1.16.0 introduces NamespaceQueue and the fairshare plugin. Tenants can use hierarchical queues within their own namespaces to organize quotas and queue hierarchies within administrator-authorized resource pools. Fairshare brings historical resource consumption into scheduling decisions among namespaces sharing a queue, improving fairness across teams. This release also expands the HyperNode ecosystem. Platforms using other schedulers can deploy the HyperNode controller on its own to discover topology and manage supernodes and their hierarchy, then integrate that information through the HyperNode API. For inference services using Volcano, new PodGroup topology anti-affinity rules can spread instances across supernodes to reduce exposure to a shared failure domain. Scheduler performance improvements include an Unschedulable Job Cache that records why Jobs could not be scheduled and skips repeated checks until blocking conditions change. Node scoring, cache updates, and queue lookups also become more efficient. The release additionally brings Kubernetes 1.36 support, load estimation for bulk Pod dispatch, DRA scoring, and accelerator and stability improvements. Highlights Scheduler Performance and Scalability : An unschedulable Job cache reduces backlog retries, alongside improvements to node scoring, cache updates, and queue lookups. Namespace-local Queue Hierarchies : Tenants can manage hierarchical queues, quotas, and resource sharing within their namespaces and administrator-authorized resource pools. Long-Term Fairness with fairshare : Slurm-inspired usage decay improves fairness for tenants isolated by namespace and sharing a queue. PodGroup Topology Anti-Affinity : Required and preferred rules separate workload instances across HyperNode domains. A Broader HyperNode Ecosystem : Other schedulers can reuse topology discovery and supernode management without running the other Volcano components. Key Features 1. Scheduler performance and scalability v1.16.0 introduces the Unschedulable Job Cache to improve scheduling under large pending backlogs, alongside improvements to node scoring, cache updates, and queue lookups. Unschedulable Job Cache A Job may remain Pending because its queue is full, the cluster lacks suitable resources, or no node satisfies its placement constraints. Repeating the same scheduling checks in every session adds work without changing that outcome. With a large backlog, these retries also compete with newly submitted Jobs that could run. The new UnschedulableJobCache records why a Job could not be scheduled. Plugins provide event hints that identify changes which could make the Job schedulable. Subsequent sessions skip the checks covered by the cached result until a relevant change requests a retry. This reduces redundant work and improves scheduling performance in clusters with persistent unschedulable backlogs. Key capabilities : Selective skipping : Uses rejection causes to skip enqueue checks, whole-Job evaluation, or checks for particular tasks while respecting gang requirements. Event-driven wakeups : A Node label update can wake a Job blocked by node affinity. Resource release or a Queue change can wake Jobs blocked by resources or quota. Storage and DRA events are also supported through plugin hints. Safe fallback : A Job is cached only when every rejecting plugin provides a safe hint. Other Jobs continue through normal per-session evaluation. Preserved scheduling semantics : Cached Jobs remain visible to pending demand, queue accounting, and gang requirements. Normal checks run again before placement after a wakeup. Bounded retries : A watchdog retries cached Jobs after a configurable maximum skip duration, defaulting to five minutes. The in-memory cache is cleared on scheduler restart. The feature is disabled by default. Enable it with the scheduler feature gate: helm upgrade --install volcano volcano-sh/volcano \ --namespace volcano-system --create-namespace --version 1.16.0 \ --set custom.scheduler_feature_gates="UnschedulableJobCache=true" Initial coverage includes the upstream predicates integrated by Volcano, native Resource Fit, proportion, and non-hierarchical capacity. Hierarchical capacity rejections and rejections from plugins without hint providers continue to be evaluated each session. Optional per-Job debug metrics report skips, wakeups, and watchdog expirations. Related: PRs: #5848 , #5644 Design and performance results: Unschedulable Job Cache User guide: Enable the Unschedulable Job Cache Contributor: @ JesseStutler Multiple scoring plugins can now score nodes in a shared traversal, reducing scoring overhead when several plugins are active. Node updates and queue lookups also avoid unnecessary object copying and traversal. ( #5928 , #5556 , #5506 ) Volcano will continue to improve performance and scalability. Future work will explore scheduling efficiency, cache and event processing, and status updates, guided by workload benchmarks and production feedback. 2. NamespaceQueue brings queue hierarchies to Namespaces Platforms use different tenancy models. Some assign resource pools to tenants through cluster-scoped Queues. Others use namespaces as the management boundary for teams or projects and want tenants to configure queue quotas and hierarchies within that boundary. NamespaceQueue supports this namespace-based model, aligning queue management with tenant ownership. NamespaceQueue introduces a namespaced resource with the same resource-governance concepts as Queue, including capability, deserved, guarantee , and reclaimable . Administrators authorize a namespace to attach its queue hierarchy to a cluster Queue through spec.allowedNamespaces . Tenants can then manage their own hierarchy within that boundary. This separates resource-pool authorization from day-to-day tenant queue management. Different namespaces can use the same queue names without sharing queue identity. The feature is disabled by default. The Helm switch enables the participating controller, scheduler, and admission components and selects hierarchical capacity when using the chart’s default scheduler configuration: helm upgrade --install volcano volcano-sh/volcano \ --namespace volcano-system --create-namespace --version 1.16.0 \ --set custom.namespace_queue_enable=true Create the namespace and authorized parent Queue, then the tenant queue: apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: team-a --- apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1 kind: Queue metadata: name: research spec: capability: cpu: "100" memory: "200Gi" deserved: cpu: "100" memory: "200Gi" allowedNamespaces: - team-a --- apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1 kind: NamespaceQueue metadata: name: training namespace: team-a spec: parent: cluster/research capability: cpu: "40" memory: "80Gi" deserved: cpu: "40" memory: "80Gi" reclaimable: true Grant tenant RBAC permissions for namespacequeues in the tenant’s namespace. After the NamespaceQueue reports Ready=True and Authorized=True , Jobs and PodGroups in team-a can reference it with: spec: queue: namespace/training Bare names still reference cluster Queues. cluster/<name> identifies a cluster Queue parent, while an unprefixed parent name identifies a NamespaceQueue in the same namespace. Initial scheduling support uses hierarchical capacity. Do not enable proportion alongside it. Related: PRs: #5590 , #5629 User guide: NamespaceQueue Design: Namespace-scoped Queues Contributor: @ gitGurugu 3. fairshare improves long-term tenant fairness Volcano traditionally organizes resource sharing and quota governance around cluster-scoped Queues, which fits deployments that assign a dedicated queue to each tenant. Other platforms use namespaces as the isolation boundary for teams or projects, with multiple tenants submitting into one Queue.
